content: Actin is a globular protein with a molecular weight of approximately 42 kDa, found in all eukaryotic cells except nematode sperm. It is present in high concentrations, often exceeding 100 μM, and is one of the most highly conserved proteins across species, with less than 20% variation between organisms as diverse as algae and humans. Actin serves as the monomeric subunit of microfilaments, which are one of the three primary components of the cytoskeleton, and is also a key component of thin filaments in muscle cells. These structural roles enable actin to participate in a wide range of cellular functions, including muscle contraction, cell motility, cell division, cytokinesis, vesicle and organelle transport, cell signaling, and the maintenance of cell shape and junctions. Actin filaments are linked to α-actinin and the cell membrane through vinculin at cadherin-based adherens junctions. The head domain of vinculin interacts with E-cadherin via α-, β-, and γ-catenins, while its tail domain binds to membrane lipids and actin filaments. Actin's evolutionary conservation is remarkable, with 80.2% sequence conservation at the gene level between humans and the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, and 95% conservation of the protein's primary structure. While most yeast species have a single actin gene, higher eukaryotes express multiple isoforms encoded by a family of related genes. Mammals, for instance, have at least six actin isoforms, categorized into alpha, beta, and gamma classes based on their isoelectric points. Alpha actins are predominantly found in muscle tissues (e.g., α-skeletal, α-aortic smooth, α-cardiac, and γ2-enteric smooth), while beta and gamma isoforms are more common in non-muscle cells (e.g., βand γ1-cytoplasmic). Despite their similar amino acid sequences and in vitro properties, these isoforms are not fully interchangeable in vivo. The typical actin gene consists of a 100-nucleotide 5' untranslated region (UTR), a 1200-nucleotide coding region, and a 200-nucleotide 3' UTR. Most actin genes contain introns, with up to six introns located in 19 well-characterized positions. Actin's high conservation makes it a model for studying intron evolution, particularly in the context of the introns-early and introns-late hypotheses. Non-spherical prokaryotes possess actin homologs, such as MreB, which are essential for maintaining cell shape. Additionally, the plasmid-derived gene ParM encodes an actin-like protein that exhibits dynamic instability and facilitates plasmid DNA segregation during cell division, akin to the role of microtubules in eukaryotic mitosis. Actin is also found in both smooth and rough endoplasmic reticulum. Actin has three primary functions in cells. First, it forms the most dynamic component of the cytoskeleton, providing mechanical support and facilitating signal transduction. Second, it enables cell motility, as seen in actoclampin molecular motors. Third, in both muscle and non-muscle cells, actin interacts with myosin to generate force for processes such as muscle contraction, vesicle transport, and other intracellular movements. Actin subunits, known as globular actin (G-actin), polymerize into filamentous actin (F-actin), which forms long, helical microfilaments. These microfilaments, approximately 7 nm in diameter, consist of two parallel F-actin strands twisted into a helix with a repeating loop every 37 nm. Actin filaments exhibit polarity, with barbed (+) and pointed (-) ends, which can be visualized by decorating the filaments with myosin S1 fragments. These fragments consist of the head and neck domains of myosin II. In muscle cells, actin is the primary component of thin filaments, which, together with myosin-based thick filaments, form actomyosin myofibrils. These myofibrils drive muscle contraction through a cycle powered by ATP hydrolysis. Myosin heads attach to actin filaments, exert tension, and perform a power stroke that slides the thin filaments past the thick filaments, shortening the muscle. In contractile bundles, the actin-bundling protein α-actinin maintains a spacing of approximately 35 nm between thin filaments, allowing thick filaments to interact and facilitate contraction. During deformation, myosin binds to the plasma membrane at one end and walks toward the plus end of an actin filament at the other, reshaping the membrane relative to the cell cortex. In contraction, myosin binds to two separate filaments and moves both ends toward their respective plus ends, sliding the filaments closer together and shortening the actin bundle. This mechanism underlies muscle contraction and cytokinesis, the process of dividing one cell into two. Actin polymerization and depolymerization are also critical for chemotaxis and cytokinesis, with nucleating factors required to initiate polymerization. Actin filaments bind ATP, and ATP hydrolysis destabilizes the polymer, facilitating dynamic remodeling. The history of actin research dates back to 1887, when W.D. Halliburton extracted a protein from muscle that coagulated myosin preparations, which he termed myosin-ferment. However, the discovery of actin is credited to Brúnó F. Straub, who, in 1942, developed a method to isolate substantial amounts of pure actin while working in Albert Szent-Györgyi's laboratory. Straub's method, still in use today, revealed that actin could activate myosin, leading to its naming. During World War II, the findings were not widely disseminated until 1945, when they were published in Acta Physiologica Scandinavica. In 1950, Straub reported that actin binds ATP, which is hydrolyzed to ADP and inorganic phosphate during polymerization. This ATP-to-ADP transition was later linked to muscle contraction, particularly in smooth muscle, though experimental confirmation came only in 2001. The crystal structure of G-actin was solved in 1990 by Kabsch and colleagues, and a model for F-actin was proposed by Holmes and colleagues the same year. Despite advances, a high-resolution X-ray structure of F-actin remains elusive. Interestingly, the bacterium Listeria exploits actin polymerization via its ActA transmembrane protein to propel itself within host cells, demonstrating the versatility of actin's cellular functions.
